title: Anatomical position and directional terms
blurb: Describe the anatomical position and use each pair of directional terms correctly, including the limb and forearm cases the exam loves.
question: A patient lying on his back has a cut on his forearm on the thumb side, closer to the wrist than the elbow. Which directional terms describe the cut's location, and why does it not matter that he is lying down?

teach.h: One standard pose for every description
teach.body: Anatomical position is the reference pose for all directional terms: body upright, facing forward, feet flat and pointing forward, arms at the sides, palms facing forward (anterior), thumbs pointing away from the body. Plain English: stand tall, look ahead, and turn your palms to the front. Every term is read from this pose, even when the patient is lying down.

teach.h: Check the pose, top to bottom
items: Body upright, head and eyes facing forward.
Thumbs pointing away from the body (laterally).
Feet flat on the floor and pointing forward.

teach.body: Directional terms describe where one structure is relative to another, so they always come in opposite pairs and always use the patient's own body as the reference. Because they are fixed to anatomical position, the words do not change when a patient sits, lies face up or lies face down. 'Superior' still means toward the head, wherever the head happens to be pointing.

head: Term pair
Meaning
Example
rows: Closer to / farther from limb attachment
teach.caption: Synonyms: superior = cranial, inferior = caudal, anterior = ventral, posterior = dorsal.

teach.h: Sort the pairs by what they measure
teach.caption: Ipsilateral and contralateral compare sides: same side or opposite side of the body.

teach.h: Proximal and distal belong to limbs
teach.body: Proximal means closer to where a limb attaches to the trunk (or to the origin of a structure); distal means farther away. Use them along the arm and leg: the knee is proximal to the ankle. On the trunk, use superior and inferior instead. And in humans, ventral simply means anterior and dorsal means posterior: ventral does not mean 'lower'.

teach.h: Down the arm: proximal to distal
teach.caption: Any structure is proximal to everything after it in this chain and distal to everything before it.

teach.h: The forearm trap: radius versus ulna
teach.caption: This only works because the palms face forward in anatomical position, which puts the thumbs on the outside.

teach.body: Mr. Alvarez lies face up in bed with a cut on his forearm, on the thumb side, nearer the wrist. His student nurse, Brianna, charts it as on the lateral forearm, distal to the elbow and proximal to the wrist. She ignores how he is lying: in anatomical position the palms face forward, so the thumb side is lateral, and the terms stay the same in any posture.

teach.text: Watch for: proximal and distal used on the trunk or reversed (the knee is PROXIMAL to the ankle); the radius called medial (it is lateral, on the thumb side); and ventral read as 'lower' (it means anterior).

items: Anatomical position: upright, facing forward, palms forward, thumbs out, feet forward.
Terms refer to anatomical position whatever the patient's real posture.
Medial/lateral = toward/away from midline; the radius is lateral to the ulna.
Proximal/distal = closer to/farther from limb attachment; superficial/deep = surface.

summary: You can now describe the anatomical position and use every pair of directional terms from it, whatever the patient's posture. You can also handle the classic traps: proximal and distal on limbs, the lateral radius, and ventral meaning anterior.

A.q: In anatomical position, which way do the palms face?
A.why: In anatomical position the arms hang at the sides with the palms facing forward and the thumbs pointing away from the body.

whyNot.0: Palms toward the thighs is the relaxed standing pose, not anatomical position.
whyNot.2: Palms facing backward is the reverse of anatomical position, which has them facing forward.
whyNot.3: Palms face the floor only when the arms are held out in front; that is not anatomical position.

A.q: Which word correctly completes the statement? The elbow is ____ to the wrist.
A.why: Along a limb, the structure closer to the trunk attachment is proximal: the elbow is nearer the shoulder than the wrist is.

whyNot.0: Distal is the reverse: the wrist is distal to the elbow.
whyNot.1: Lateral compares distance from the midline, not position along a limb.
whyNot.2: Superficial compares depth from the body surface, not position along a limb.

A.q: Which directional term means toward the midline of the body?
A.why: Medial means toward the midline; lateral means away from it.

whyNot.1: Lateral is the opposite of medial: away from the midline.
whyNot.2: Proximal means closer to where a limb attaches to the trunk.
whyNot.3: Ipsilateral means on the same side of the body.

B.q: In anatomical position, which statement is CORRECT?
options: The radius is medial to the ulna
The ulna is lateral to the radius
The radius is lateral to the ulna
The thumb is medial to the little finger
B.why: With the palms facing forward, the thumb side of the forearm is lateral, and the radius is on the thumb side.

whyNot.0: This reverses the bones: the radius is the lateral one.
whyNot.1: The ulna is on the little-finger side, which is medial.
whyNot.3: In anatomical position the thumb points away from the body, so it is lateral to the little finger.

B.q: Which word correctly completes the statement? The sternum is ____ to the heart.
B.why: The sternum (breastbone) lies in front of the heart, so it is anterior to it.

whyNot.1: Posterior means behind; the vertebral column, not the sternum, lies behind the heart.
whyNot.2: Deep means farther from the surface; the sternum is closer to the surface than the heart.
whyNot.3: The sternum and heart are at the same chest level; the key relationship is front to back.

B.q: A patient lies face down on an exam table. A nurse notes a mole between the shoulder blades. Which term describes the mole's location?
B.why: The back of the body is dorsal (posterior). The patient's posture does not change the term.

whyNot.0: Ventral means anterior (front), even though the back now faces the ceiling.
whyNot.1: Inferior means toward the feet; the shoulder blades are on the upper back.
whyNot.3: Distal is used along limbs, not to describe the trunk.

C.q: Which statement uses directional terms CORRECTLY?
options: The knee is distal to the ankle
The ears are medial to the eyes
The skin is deep to the skeletal muscles
The heart is superior to the diaphragm
C.why: The heart sits above the diaphragm, closer to the head, so it is superior to it.

whyNot.0: The knee is closer to the hip, so it is proximal to the ankle.
whyNot.1: The ears are farther from the midline than the eyes, so they are lateral.
whyNot.2: The skin is nearer the surface, so it is superficial to the muscles.

C.q: A report states that a patient's right hand is contralateral to his left foot. What does contralateral mean?
options: On the same side of the body as it
On the opposite side of the body
Closer to the attachment of the limb
Farther from the surface of the body
C.why: Contralateral means on the opposite side; the right hand and left foot are on opposite sides.

whyNot.0: Same side is ipsilateral, the opposite of contralateral.
whyNot.2: Closer to the limb attachment is proximal.
whyNot.3: Farther from the surface is deep.

C.q: Jada documents an injection site as distal to the shoulder and proximal to the elbow. Which regional term names this site?
C.why: Between the shoulder and the elbow is the upper arm, the brachial region.

whyNot.0: Antecubital is the front of the elbow itself, not the area above it.
whyNot.1: Carpal is the wrist, which is distal to the elbow.
whyNot.3: Axillary is the armpit, at the shoulder where the limb meets the trunk.

reteach.title: Think of a map that always points north
reteach.question: A map is printed north-up. If you turn it upside down, is north still north? How does that match the way directional terms work on a patient?

blocks.h: A fixed reference beats your viewpoint
blocks.body: Map directions are tied to the map, not to how you hold it. Turn it around and Chicago is still north of St. Louis. Anatomical position is the body's north-up map. Once you picture the patient standing with palms forward, every term is fixed: lie the patient down, roll them over, and the forehead is still superior to the chin.

blocks.text: Use the patient's right and left, not yours. Facing a patient, their right side is on your left.

explain.body: Upright, facing forward, feet forward, arms at sides, palms forward, thumbs out. All terms refer to this pose, even for a patient lying down.

test.q: A patient is lying on her back. When the nurse charts a wound with directional terms, the terms are based on
options: the nurse's own point of view
the side of the bed she faces
test.why: Directional terms always refer to anatomical position, whatever the patient's real posture.

whyNot.0: The patient's actual posture does not change the terms.
whyNot.2: Terms use the patient's body as the reference, never the observer's viewpoint.
whyNot.3: The bed and room do not affect anatomical terms.

explain.body: Superior (cranial) = toward the head; inferior (caudal) = toward the feet. Anterior (ventral) = front; posterior (dorsal) = back.

test.q: Which pair of terms are synonyms in human anatomy?
test.why: In humans, ventral and anterior both mean the front of the body.

whyNot.2: Cranial means superior (toward the head), not posterior.
whyNot.3: Caudal means inferior (toward the feet), the opposite of superior.

explain.body: Medial = toward the midline; lateral = away from it. The nose is medial to the eyes; the ears are lateral to the eyes; the radius is lateral to the ulna.

test.q: Which word correctly completes the statement? The nose is ____ to the cheeks.
test.why: The nose lies on the midline, so it is medial to the cheeks on either side.

whyNot.0: Lateral would put the nose farther from the midline than the cheeks.
whyNot.1: Proximal and distal describe positions along limbs, not the face.
whyNot.2: Contralateral means on the opposite side; the nose is on the midline.

explain.body: Proximal = closer to the limb's attachment; distal = farther. Superficial = toward the surface; deep = away from it. The fingers are distal to the wrist; skin is superficial to muscle.

options: The wrist is proximal to the elbow
The ankle is proximal to the knee
The fingers are distal to the wrist
The muscle is superficial to the skin
test.why: The fingers are farther from the limb's attachment at the shoulder than the wrist is, so they are distal.

whyNot.0: The wrist is farther from the shoulder than the elbow, so it is distal to the elbow.
whyNot.1: The ankle is farther from the hip than the knee, so it is distal to the knee.
whyNot.3: Muscle lies under the skin, so it is deep to the skin.
